claims.text: Prior art: Swift arrays are copy-on-write value types; hidden copies led Swift to add `isKnownUniquelyReferenced`, and the ownership proposals SE-0366 (`consume`) and SE-0377 (`borrowing`/`consuming`) to control copies explicitly.

evidence.source: Swift Evolution SE-0366, SE-0377
evidence.detail: Swift kept value semantics but added tools to make copies controllable

claims.text: Prior art: Koka (Perceus, Reinking et al. PLDI 2021) and Lean 4 keep an immutable API and update in place when the reference count is 1 ('functional but in-place'); a shared value is copied silently, as in Narra today.

evidence.source: Perceus: Garbage Free Reference Counting with Reuse (PLDI 2021); Lean 4 Array docs
evidence.detail: in-place reuse removes the cost for unique values but does not show copies in the source

claims.text: Prior art: OCaml and Reason have mutable arrays and `ref` with reference semantics, made safe by a tracing GC; most data (lists, records) is immutable by default. Hylo uses mutable value semantics with `inout` and makes copies explicit (`.copy()`) instead of copy-on-write. Rust moves on assignment and requires `.clone()`.

evidence.source: OCaml manual; Hylo language tour; Rust book
evidence.detail: explicit copy appears in Hylo and Rust; reference semantics with mutation in OCaml relies on a GC

claims.text: Keep value semantics and TypeScript in-place syntax (`items[i] = v`, `p.hp = 0`, `Arrays.push(mutable xs, v)`, `mutable` arguments, `for (mutable ...)`), and add one compile rule, the shared write: an in-place change to an array, map or struct that the checker cannot prove unshared is an error whose fix writes the copy. `let a = [1]; const b = a; a[0] = 9; log(b)` stops compiling with the hint `const b = Arrays.copy(a)`, so TypeScript-valid code either means the same or does not compile (D2), and no copy happens that the source does not show.

evidence.source: Hylo language tour (no implicit copies of non-trivial values, `.copy()` and moves at last use); Swift SE-0377 (`borrowing`/`consuming` parameters are not implicitly copyable, the `copy x` operator makes the copy explicit); J10, J12
evidence.detail: Hylo and Swift ownership both keep value semantics and in-place mutation and make copies explicit by rejecting the implicit copy at compile time; neither needed reference semantics or immutable-by-default collections to do it

claims.text: Sharing is decided per function body with no annotations and no lifetimes: `const b = a` moves when `a` is not used afterwards and shares otherwise; a name read out of a place (`const xs = game.players`), a plain parameter, a pattern or `for (const ...)` binding, a by-value capture and `Cells.get` share with their source while it is live; a call result is fresh unless the callee can return part of a parameter, a flag the checker infers per function (a callee change surfaces as a compile error at callers, never as a silent copy, which answers D46's objection to inference). In the corpus, 843 locals start from a plain path, 19 of them are later changed in place and 12 of those keep the source live; 131 locals from calls are changed, 82 from `Str.builder` and the rest from 30 constructors that build fresh values.

claims.text: `mutable` parameters, `for (mutable ...)` and `Cell<T>` keep their syntax; only their hidden-copy clause changes: a `mutable` argument or loop source that is shared is a compile error instead of a copy, so D27's 'no copies' becomes a guarantee. No `ref` and no mutable array type are added: `Cell` is already `ref` (J6), and an `Array<T>` held by one name is the mutable array. `Cells.get` shares with the cell, so changing its result needs `Arrays.copy` (D90's O(n) per update becomes visible), and a new `Cells.modify(cell, (mutable value) => { Arrays.push(mutable value, x) })` for contents types moves the value out of the box for the call so the change is in place. A large array is therefore never cloned unless `Arrays.copy` is written, which answers the weakness the maintainer noted in `ref`.

claims.text: The three explicit copy forms are shallow. Structs live inline and a copy only counts their boxed fields (SPEC section 6), so `{ ...checker }` shares all 49 Array/Map fields of Checker, and `Arrays.copy` of an array of structs shares each element's arrays. The next nested write, `copy.bodies[i].closures[j] = x`, is a shared write again. A deep copy fixes that but copies the whole tree up front, where copy on write today copies only the path that is written. For isolation copies such as a hover query over the checker, that turns a lazy copy into an eager one of every array.

evidence.source: grep of struct Checker fields in selfhost/src/check.nra:405; SPEC.md section 6 "Values and ownership"
evidence.detail: evidence/opponent-copy-and-calibration.txt

claims.text: `Cells.modify` moves the value out of the box while the callback runs, but every copy of a Cell handle shares the slot (D90). A callback that reaches the same cell through another handle, captured or stored in a struct, finds the slot empty, and no local rule can see that two handles are the same cell. The only ways out are a runtime check that panics, which D92 forbids, or a fallback copy, which is the hidden copy the goal removes. Swift had to enforce exclusivity at runtime for class properties, globals and escaping closures (SE-0176), and Rust's RefCell panics on a second borrow_mut, for the same reason.

evidence.source: Swift SE-0176 Enforce Exclusive Access to Memory; Rust std::cell::RefCell; DECISIONS.md D90, D92
evidence.detail: static exclusivity could not cover shared handles in Swift; dynamic checks trap at runtime

claims.text: Errors that depend on liveness move when code changes elsewhere: adding `log(b)` at the end of a function turns an earlier, accepted `a[0] = 9` into an error. Rust's lexical borrow checker rejected so much correct code that NLL (RFC 2094) took years to fix it, Polonius is still unfinished, and Rust's annual surveys list the borrow checker among the hardest parts to learn. Hylo, the closest model, is still experimental with no production users, so there is no user evidence for it yet. Errors should state the later use that causes them.

evidence.source: Rust RFC 2094 (non-lexical lifetimes); rust-lang/polonius; Rust annual survey results; hylo-lang.org
evidence.detail: liveness-based acceptance was needed to cut false rejections, and the diagnostics point at a use far from the error

claims.text: Keep P1's shared-write rule but make it local and visible in signatures, with no inference: (1) liveness only inside one body; (2) parameters, pattern, for and captured bindings are always shared; (3) a call result is fresh unless the callee's signature marks the result as sharing a parameter (about 16 functions in the corpus, checked inside the callee as D46 checks `escaping`); (4) one `copy(x)` that works at any depth, and a value it produced may be written: the copy sits at the `copy` site and the runtime copy on write does the work lazily, path by path, so a nested copy is never eager (O4). No fixpoint and no re-checking of callers in the LSP. Step 2 then costs about what P7 claims for it, and the copy check of P4 still holds the runtime at zero implicit copies.

claims.text: P2 is amended: no cross-function inference. Liveness stays inside one body; a call result is fresh unless the callee's signature carries the `from` marker of P10; the precision P2 left out is spelled out in P9.

The analysis runs in the checker after types are known, one body at a time, and tracks only values whose type has contents (D81 rule 1 types and structs with boxed fields); strings, scalars and enums are never tracked. Facts are 'name N shares place path X'. A plain parameter, a pattern or `for (const ...)` binding, a by-value capture and a value from an identity type (`Cells.get`, `await`, a received message) always share. Assigning a place path rooted at a local or a `mutable` parameter ends the facts on that path (a strong update, sound because both are exclusive), so the 72 save/restore sites (`const savedLabels = checker.labels; checker.labels = []; ...; checker.labels = savedLabels`) pass unchanged. A store into a literal (`S { items: xs }`) is a move when `xs` is dead on that path, and a `return` ends the path, so 0 of 8 sampled literal-then-write sites need an edit. Generic `T` and `Dynamic` need no rule because D81 rule 8 already forbids changing them in place. Liveness follows loop back edges, and each error names the later use that causes it, which answers O6: `a[0] = 9 changes a value that b still uses at line 14; write const b = copy(a), or stop using b first`.

claims.text: The signature marker is `from` after the result type, naming the parameters the result may share: `function parameterTypes(signature: Signature): Array<Type> from signature` and `function mergeSort(items: Array<SortItem>): Array<SortItem> from items`. Inside the callee, returning a value that shares a parameter without `from` is a compile error with two fixes (add `from items`, or return `copy(items)`), checked as D46 checks `escaping`. At the call, the result shares the `from` arguments while they are live, so `let sorted = mergeSort(items)` at the last use of `items` is free to change and before it is a shared write. Callers depend only on signatures, so the LSP re-checks callers only when a signature changes. About 16 functions in the corpus take the mark.

claims.text: P4 is amended: the three shallow copy forms are dropped as copy tools and one prelude `copy(x)` replaces them (P12). The debug copy check and the removal of `--report-copies`, `NARRA_TRACE_COPIES` and `@unique` stay.

`copy(x)` is a prelude function for any type with contents (on a string, scalar or enum it is a compile error: nothing to copy). At runtime it is one retain: O(1) at the call site, returning the same object. Its result counts as unshared for the checker, so writes to it and to `x` are both accepted; the existing copy-on-write then copies only the nodes on the path each write touches, once each, so `const c = copy(checker); c.bodies[i].closures[j] = x` copies Checker, one array of bodies and one array of closures, not all 49 arrays (O4). For the debug copy check of P4 to stay at zero, debug builds keep a side set of objects shared by a `copy`: `copy` adds `x`'s object, a copy-on-write of a member also adds the member's children, and only a copy of an object outside the set is reported at exit (exit code like the leak check's 102). Release builds have no set and no header change (`rc` stays one `int64_t`).

claims.text: P9 never says that a `mutable R` argument writes everything reachable from R, and the sound version of P9 must treat it that way. That rule rejects the commonest pattern in the compiler: a local read out of the context, a helper called with `mutable` context, then the local used again. Examples: `const info = emitter.checker.consts[constIndex]`, then `startFunction(mutable emitter, ...)`, then `info.module` (emitconsts.nra:149-158), and `const body = checker.bodies[bodyIndex]` in query.nra:484. There are 79 such sites with a contents-typed path and up to 138 with mixed field names, about 4 to 7 times P2's 20. Leaving the rule out instead is unsound: the callee can change that path, TypeScript would show the change through the local, and Narra copies silently. The runtime fix is cheap, since `copy` is O(1) under P12, but it is about 100 more edits and one more source of `copy` noise.

claims.text: P12's runtime story is sound in release. After `const c = copy(x)` a write to `x` copies x's node by copy on write and `c` keeps the old value, which is the intended meaning, and release builds add no header and no set. The debug set is weaker than P12 says, for two reasons. It records objects, not copy sites, so once an object has passed through `copy`, any later implicit copy of it or of its copied children is exempt for the object's whole life, and an analysis hole on that object goes unreported. And `narra_free` has no per-object hook today, so the set needs one to drop freed addresses before malloc reuses them, or new objects inherit the exemption.

claims.text: P9's claims that every struct with only scalars is safe to skip and that the save/restore sites pass unchanged are withdrawn. P17 states the rule with the three additions, and the extra 100 to 170 sites go into the sweep (P20).

Final rule. Tracked values: every struct (all-scalar ones like `Pos` too), array, map, `FixedArray`, `Box`, `StringBuilder`, generator and coroutine; strings, scalars and enums never. (1) A write to place P conflicts with every live name that shares P's root or a proper prefix of P; the check runs first, and only then are the facts on P and below cleared. So `const b = a; a.items = []` is an error (b shares the container), while `const saved = checker.labels; checker.labels = []` is not (saved keeps the old array, as in TypeScript). (2) Passing `mutable R` is a write to R and to every path below R. Passing `mutable R.f` is a write only to R.f and below. (3) Each error names the write, the sharing name and its later use, and carries a fix that `narrac apply-fix` can apply: put `copy(...)` around the initialiser of the sharing name. Copying is O(1) (P12), so the fix is always safe. Before: `const info = emitter.checker.consts[constIndex]` ... `startFunction(mutable emitter, ...)` ... `constName(info.module, info.name)`; error `startFunction(mutable emitter, ...) may change emitter.checker.consts[constIndex], which info still uses at line 158`. After: `const info = copy(emitter.checker.consts[constIndex])`, or the second fix, which reads the field after the call. At save/restore sites, the second fix moves the reset above the first `mutable` call.

claims.text: P17's rule (1) is written in one direction and misses two D2 forms. (a) A write through the alias while the source is live: in `const items = a.items; items[0] = 9; log(a.items)` the write's root is `items`, and with the fact 'items shares a.items' no live name shares `items`. The facts have to be symmetric, so a later read of `a`, of `a.items` or of a path between them conflicts, and transitive, for `const c = b` after `const b = a`. (b) A non-escaping closure that writes a captured `const` by reference (D81 rule 9): in `const b = a; Arrays.forEach(xs, (x) => { a[0] = x }); log(b)` the write sits in the closure body, so passing that closure has to count as a write to `a` at the call. Each needs a rule line and an error sample in step 5.

claims.text: The credit scheme is sound only with more hooks than P18 states. It removes an entry 'when the count falls back to 1', but counts fall in about 12 runtime sites (runtimecore, runtimemap, runtimestdstring, runtimeclosureenv) and in the per-type release and unique code that emitdecls.nra generates, not in `narra_free`. With only the free hook, `const c = copy(x)` dropped unwritten leaves x's credit until x is freed, so a later analysis hole on x goes unreported, which is O12's weakness for that case. Once the decrement hooks exist (debug only), the remaining gap is small: a credit can be used up by the wrong holder, so at most one hidden copy per `copy` call goes unreported. That is acceptable.
